# MEMORANDUM

**TO:** Supervising Partner
**FROM:** [Associate]
**DATE:** November 27, 2026
**RE:** Rekaind Vertical Services, Inc. / Velert Systems, LLC: review of the LiftSense license documents (Licensor Ref. VS-REK-2025-001)

---

## I. Executive Summary

I reviewed all seven documents in the folder:

- the Software License Agreement effective March 3, 2025 (the **SLA**);
- the Service Level Schedule (**SLS**);
- Order Form No. 001 (**Order Form**);
- the May 12, 2025 Side Letter (**Side Letter**);
- Rekaind's October 21, 2026 termination notice (**Notice**);
- Rekaind's dispatch-center office lease; and
- Velert's November 2, 2026 certificate of insurance.

**Commercial baseline.** The Order Form covers 1,140 elevator and escalator units in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware. The **Annual Subscription Fee is $410,400** ($360 per Licensed Unit per year). The Initial Order Term is 36 months from March 3, 2025.

**Order of precedence.** Under SLA §15.4 the documents rank as follows: Side Letter, then Order Form, then the SLA body, then the SLS. **Where the Order Form conflicts with the SLA, "the Order Form shall control."** This ranking drives two of the issues below.

**Six issues.** The most urgent is Issue 1.

1. **The Notice was late.** The chronic-failure termination was likely ineffective. Rekaind announced it would stop paying fees from November 20, 2026, a date that has now passed.
2. **The liability cap now covers Velert's bodily-injury indemnity.** The Side Letter moved Velert's bodily-injury and property-damage indemnity into a new §10.2. SLA §11.4 still carves out only §10.1. Passenger-injury claims are therefore capped at about $410,400.
3. **Ohio law and an Ohio forum displace Delaware.** Order Form §7 picks Ohio law and Franklin County courts, and it controls through §15.4.
4. **The exclusivity covenant is overbroad.** SLA §3.4 and §1.6 reach every unit Rekaind or its affiliates service worldwide, and they bar in-house development.
5. **Velert can assign freely.** Under SLA §14.2 Velert may assign without consent, including to a competing OEM. Rekaind needs consent to assign.
6. **The renewal terms are a trap.** Renewal runs for successive 36-month terms. The opt-out window is 15 days, and fees can rise by up to 7%.

The office lease and the insurance certificate raise no issues. They are addressed in Part IV.

---

## II. Summary Table

| # | Issue | Location | Why it matters | Recommended fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Termination notice sent after the 30-day window | SLS §4.2; Notice ¶¶2.3, 3.1, 5.2 | Termination likely ineffective. Stopping payment risks breach and repudiation. | Reserve rights, preserve payments, serve a fresh notice on later failing months and/or a §12.4 breach notice |
| 2 | Bodily-injury indemnity now under the cap | SLA §11.4(a) and §11.3; Side Letter §2 (new §10.2) | Passenger-injury indemnity capped at about $410,400 | Amend §11.4(a) (and §11.5) to cover new §10.1 and §10.2 |
| 3 | Ohio law and Franklin County venue override Delaware | Order Form §7; SLA §15.4 (and §§15.1–15.2) | Rekaind must litigate in Velert's home court under Ohio law | Delete Order Form §7, or carve governing law and forum out of §15.4 |
| 4 | Worldwide, affiliate-wide exclusivity | SLA §3.4; §1.6 | Blocks growth, OEM or customer-mandated tools, in-house builds and transition | Limit to Licensed Units; delete "develop" and the affiliate and hardware reach |
| 5 | One-sided assignment right | SLA §14.2 (vs. §14.1) | License, data and exclusivity could pass to a competitor | Consent, or a termination right and data protections, on assignment or change of control to a competitor |
| 6 | 36-month evergreen with a 15-day opt-out | SLA §12.2; §1.14; §12.3; Order Form §2 | Missing a 15-day window means three more years at up to 7% higher fees | Annual renewals, a longer window, termination for convenience; calendar the dates now |

---

## III. Detailed Analysis

### Issue 1: The chronic-failure termination notice was sent after the window closed

**Location:** SLS §4.2; Notice ¶¶2.2–2.3, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.2. See also SLA §12.6.

**What the documents say.**

- **The trigger.** SLS §4.1 defines a Chronic Availability Failure as Platform Availability below 99.5% in three consecutive calendar months.
- **The deadline.** SLS §4.2 requires the termination notice to be delivered "**within thirty (30) days after delivery** of the Service Report for the third consecutive calendar month" below 99.5%.
- **The Notice's own facts.** The Notice relies on June (98.87%), July (99.12%) and August (98.41%) 2026. It recites that the August Service Report was "**delivered to us on September 4, 2026**."
- **The deadline date.** Thirty days after September 4, 2026 is **October 4, 2026**.
- **The Notice date.** The Notice is dated **October 21, 2026**, which is **17 days late**.
- **What the Notice does.** It states that Rekaind "**hereby terminates**" Order Form No. 001 effective November 20, 2026. In ¶5.2 it says Rekaind "will stop paying Fees from November 20, 2026," and that any later invoice "will be returned unpaid."

Neither document shows the problem on its own. It appears only when the SLS deadline is read against the dates recited in the Notice.

**Why it matters.**

- **The termination is likely ineffective.** It is Rekaind's asserted position only. Nothing in the file shows that Velert has accepted it. Velert's November 2, 2026 insurance certificate still treats the SLA and Order Form as live.
- **Stopping payment creates exposure.** If the Order Form survives, the Year 2 fee (prepaid through March 2, 2027) is not immediately at risk. Rekaind's real exposure is:
  - the Year 3 fee of $410,400, invoiced March 3, 2027;
  - the cancelled September 28, 2026 device order; and
  - the $115,811.51 refund it has demanded, which would not be owed.
- **A repudiation argument is available to Velert.** Velert could characterize the Notice and the announced non-payment as an anticipatory repudiation, and seek damages for the rest of the term.
- **The transition itself may be a breach.** The Notice says Rekaind is migrating monitoring of the Licensed Units to "replacement arrangements" before November 20. If the Order Form is still in effect, that migration likely breaches the exclusivity covenant in SLA §3.4 (Issue 4).
- **The remediation-plan language does not help.** SLS §4.5 says participating in the remediation plan does not affect Rekaind's rights. That provision does not extend the §4.2 deadline.
- **Today's date sharpens the risk.** The stated termination date, November 20, has passed. We need to establish at once what Rekaind has actually done with respect to cutover, invoices and devices.

**Recommended fix and next steps.**

1. **Do not let Rekaind refuse invoices or stop performance on the strength of the Notice alone.** If it has a good-faith dispute, it should use the SLA §7.3 dispute mechanism, which requires written notice before the due date and bars suspension while the dispute is pending. Alternatively, it should pay under reservation of rights.
2. **Pull the September and October 2026 Service Reports.**
   - **September report.** Under SLS §7.1 it was due within the first five Business Days of October, so it was delivered on or about October 7. If September availability was also below 99.5%, then July–September is a fresh Chronic Availability Failure, and its 30-day window ran to about early November. An argument is available that the October 21 Notice falls inside that window. However, §4.2 requires the Notice to identify the Measurement Periods relied on, and this Notice names only June–August, so the argument is weaker.
   - **October report.** It was due in early November. If October also failed, the 30-day window may still be open today, running to about the first week of December.
   - **Action.** Serve a **fresh, compliant §4.2 notice immediately** that identifies the new Measurement Periods, under an express reservation that the October 21 Notice was also effective.
3. **Preserve alternative termination grounds.**
   - **SLA §12.4 (material breach).** Serve a written breach notice describing the repeated availability and alert-delivery failures, and start the 30-day cure period. SLA §5.4 says the SLS remedies do not affect §12.4.
   - **SLA §11.2 (non-conformity).** Give notice that the Platform does not conform to the Documentation, which starts a 30-day correction period followed by a termination right.
4. **Preserve SLS §3.4 credit challenges.** The 60-day window to dispute the August Service Report expired on November 3, 2026, absent earlier notice. The September and October reports remain open.

---

### Issue 2: Velert's bodily-injury and property-damage indemnity now falls under the liability cap

**Location:** SLA §11.3 and §11.4(a); Side Letter §2 (§§2.1–2.4 and Annex 1). See also SLA §11.5 and §15.4.

**What the documents say.**

- **The original structure.** Under the original SLA, §10.1 covered both (a) IP infringement and (b) "bodily injury, death or damage to tangible property" caused by Platform or Connected Device defects, including failed entrapment alerts.
- **The cap and its carve-out.** SLA §11.3 caps each party's liability at fees paid or payable in the 12 months preceding the claim. SLA §11.4(a) removes "Licensor's **indemnification obligations under Section 10.1**" from that cap.
- **The Side Letter's restructuring.** Side Letter §2.1 deletes §10.1. It replaces it with a broadened IP indemnity as new §10.1 and moves the bodily-injury indemnity into **new Section 10.2** (Side Letter §2.3).
- **What the Side Letter left untouched.** It renumbers §§10.2–10.5 and makes "conforming changes within Section 10." It **does not amend §11.4**.
- **Which document wins.** Under SLA §15.4 the Side Letter prevails. Under Side Letter §1.4 the change applies to Third-Party Claims first asserted on or after May 12, 2025.

**Why it matters.**

- **The carve-out now covers only IP claims.** Velert's indemnity for passenger injury or death is subject to the 12-month-fees cap. That cap is about **$410,400**, plus any device fees paid in the window. A single entrapment or escalator injury claim can exceed that many times over.
- **The consequential-damages exclusion may also apply.** SLA §11.5 exempts matters described in §11.4(a)–(c). The bodily-injury indemnity may therefore also be exposed to the consequential and lost-profits exclusion.
- **The change was easy to miss.** The Side Letter presents itself as a neutral restructuring that improves the IP indemnity, and the Annex 1 renumbering table reinforces that impression.
- **Rekaind's best counter-argument.** Rekaind can argue that the restructuring was intended to be neutral, and that the failure to conform §11.4 is a scrivener's error. That is a litigation argument, not protection to rely on.
- **This is a live concern now.** The Notice describes alert-delivery failures and units placed on manual monitoring on August 27, 2026. Any resulting third-party claim would be asserted after the Side Letter took effect.
- **Insurance helps only partly.** Velert's CGL and umbrella policies name Rekaind and its Affiliates as additional insureds. That gives some direct protection for bodily-injury claims tied to Velert's products. It does not restore the uncapped contractual indemnity, and the certificate itself is "information only."

**Recommended fix.**

- Amend SLA §11.4(a) by written instrument under §15.9 to read "Licensor's indemnification obligations under Sections 10.1 and 10.2 (as inserted by the Side Letter)." Conform the cross-reference in §11.5.
- Until that amendment is signed, Rekaind should send written notice of the mutual-intent position, and any indemnity claims should be tendered under both new §10.1 and new §10.2.

---

### Issue 3: Ohio law and an exclusive Franklin County forum displace the negotiated Delaware terms

**Location:** Order Form §7.1 and §7.2; SLA §15.4. This conflicts with SLA §15.1 (Delaware law) and §15.2 (Wilmington, Delaware courts).

**What the documents say.**

- **The SLA's choice.** SLA §15.1 selects Delaware law. SLA §15.2 gives exclusive jurisdiction to the state or federal courts in Wilmington, Delaware.
- **The Order Form's choice.** Order Form §7.1 provides that "This Order Form **and the Agreement**" are governed by "the **laws of the State of Ohio**." Order Form §7.2 gives exclusive jurisdiction and venue to the courts in "**Franklin County, Ohio**," which is Velert's home county.
- **Which document wins.** SLA §15.4 provides that where the Order Form conflicts with the SLA body, "**the Order Form shall control**."

Each clause looks like routine boilerplate on its own. Read together, the Order Form overrides the Delaware choice.

**Why it matters.**

- **Rekaind would litigate on Velert's ground.** Every dispute, starting with the termination and payment dispute in Issue 1, would likely be litigated in Columbus, Ohio, under Ohio law.
- **Velert can file first.** If Rekaind stops paying, Velert can file in Franklin County and rely on the exclusive-venue clause.
- **The legal analysis shifts.** Ohio law may differ from Delaware law on repudiation, enforceability of the exclusivity covenant, and contract construction, including the scrivener's-error argument in Issue 2. All of these need to be analyzed under Ohio law as well.
- **The jury waiver still applies.** The SLA §15.3 jury waiver does not conflict with Order Form §7 and remains in force.

**Recommended fix.**

- Amend to delete Order Form §7, or revise SLA §15.4 so that governing law and forum (§§15.1–15.3) control over any Order Form.
- Bar Order Forms from changing these terms unless they expressly reference and amend §15.1 and §15.2.
- Until the documents are amended, assume Ohio law and a Franklin County forum when assessing the termination dispute.

---

### Issue 4: The exclusivity covenant reaches far beyond the 1,140 Licensed Units

**Location:** SLA §3.4, read with the definition of Covered Equipment in §1.6. Compare Order Form §1.1 and §1.4.

**What the documents say.**

- **The covenant.** SLA §3.4 provides that Licensee "**shall not license, use, or develop**, and shall cause its Affiliates not to" do so, "any remote-monitoring, condition-monitoring, dispatch or work-order software other than the Platform for any Covered Equipment."
- **The definition.** Covered Equipment means "**any equipment serviced by Licensee or any of its Affiliates anywhere in the world**" (§1.6, repeated in §3.4).
- **The hardware bar.** Section 3.4 also bars procuring any monitoring hardware that transmits data to another platform.
- **Duration.** The covenant runs for the Term and for as long as any Order Form remains in effect.
- **What is actually licensed.** The Order Form licenses only 1,140 units in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware. Units added under Order Form §1.4 must be in those three states unless the parties sign a new Order Form or an amendment.
- **No narrowing.** Nothing in the Order Form or Side Letter narrows the definition.

**Why it matters.**

- **Growth outside the three states is blocked.** Rekaind cannot use another monitoring or dispatch tool for any new contract outside the licensed footprint. It also cannot use LiftSense there without Velert agreeing to a new Order Form.
- **OEM and customer-mandated tools are barred.** Rekaind cannot use OEM-mandated or customer-mandated monitoring systems, which are common in modernization and OEM-equipment contracts. The same is true of its own dispatch and work-order tools.
- **In-house development is barred.** Rekaind cannot build its own tools. SLA §3.5(f) separately restricts using the Platform to build a competitive product.
- **The covenant binds affiliates and acquisitions.** It binds every present and future Affiliate, which could block an acquisition of, or by, another service company.
- **Transition is a breach until the term ends.** Moving to a replacement system before termination is effective breaches §3.4 (see Issue 1). The covenant's duration is also extended by the evergreen renewal (Issue 6).
- **Enforceability is uncertain.** The scope may be challengeable as an unreasonable restraint. That depends on governing law, which Issue 3 makes uncertain, and Rekaind should not rely on it.

**Recommended fix.**

- Limit §3.4 to the **Licensed Units** under an effective Order Form, and to Rekaind only rather than its Affiliates.
- Delete "develop."
- Carve out OEM-required or customer-mandated systems, acquired businesses, and transition and parallel-running activity during the final 120 days of a term or after any termination notice.
- Narrow the hardware bar the same way.
- Limit §1.6 accordingly, or delete it.

---

### Issue 5: Velert has an unrestricted right to assign

**Location:** SLA §14.2. Compare §14.1.

**What the documents say.**

- **Rekaind's position.** Under §14.1 Rekaind may not assign without Velert's consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld.
- **Velert's position.** Under §14.2 "**Licensor may assign this Agreement**," together with any or all Order Forms, "**without Licensee's consent**." This covers assignment to any Affiliate, or to any successor "by merger, consolidation, **change of control**, sale of assets, sale of equity or otherwise."
- **Notice.** Velert must give notice only within 30 days **after** the assignment takes effect.

**Why it matters.**

- **The license could land with a competitor.** Velert could transfer the license to an elevator OEM or another firm that competes with Rekaind for maintenance contracts.
- **Rekaind's data would go with it.** The transferee would hold Rekaind's Customer Data, including unit registers, building and customer contacts, maintenance histories and pricing-sensitive information.
- **Rekaind would stay locked in.** The transferee would control a platform Rekaind is bound to use exclusively under §3.4.
- **Rekaind would have no remedy.** It would have no consent right, no termination right and no advance warning.

**Recommended fix.**

- Require Rekaind's prior written consent to any assignment or change of control in favor of a **competitor**, defined to include elevator and escalator OEMs and maintenance providers.
- Alternatively, give Rekaind a right to terminate without charge, with a pro-rata refund, transition assistance under §12.8, and release from §3.4, exercisable within 90 days after notice.
- Require at least 60 days' **advance** notice of any assignment.
- Add firewall and use restrictions on Customer Data for any successor.

---

### Issue 6: Automatic renewal for 36-month terms with a 15-day opt-out window

**Location:** SLA §12.2, §1.14 and §12.3; Order Form §2.1 and §2.2.

**What the documents say.**

- **Automatic renewal.** Under §12.2 each Order Form "automatically renews" for a "**Renewal Term equal in length to the Initial Order Term**," and keeps renewing until stopped. The Order Form sets the Initial Order Term at **36 months**, ending March 2, 2028.
- **The opt-out window.** Non-renewal notice must be given within the Non-Renewal Window, which runs "**not more than seventy-five (75) days and not less than sixty (60) days**" before expiry (§1.14 and §12.2). That is a **15-day window**.
- **The current window.** For the current term, the window runs approximately December 18, 2027 to January 2, 2028. Those dates should be confirmed, but they include a holiday period.
- **Price increases.** Under §12.3 Velert may raise per-unit fees by up to **7%** for each Renewal Term on 90 days' notice.

**Why it matters.**

- **Missing the window is costly.** If Rekaind misses the window, it is locked in until March 2031 at up to $439,128 a year on the current unit count.
- **The lock-in compounds the other issues.** The exclusivity in Issue 4 extends for the same period. Rekaind would remain subject to the cap problem in Issue 2 and the Ohio forum in Issue 3.
- **Early notice is also ineffective.** A notice given earlier than 75 days before expiry falls outside the window and is arguably ineffective too.
- **Relevance today.** If the termination in Issue 1 fails, this window becomes Rekaind's next clean exit.

**Recommended fix.**

- Convert renewals to 12-month terms.
- Allow non-renewal notice at any time up to 60 days before expiry, with no earliest date.
- Add termination for convenience on 90 days' notice after the Initial Order Term.
- Cap renewal increases at the lesser of CPI or 3%.
- **Immediately:** docket the December 18, 2027 to January 2, 2028 window, with reminders.
- Consider serving a protective non-renewal notice inside the window, regardless of how the termination dispute resolves.

---

## IV. Documents Reviewed With No Issues Identified

- **Dispatch center office lease (1700 Spring Garden Street, Suite 300).** This lease has no bearing on the Velert relationship. Its terms (term through September 30, 2030, renewal notice between March 31 and September 30, 2029, Pennsylvania law) raise no issue for this matter. The renewal-notice dates should stay on Rekaind's general docket.
- **Velert certificate of insurance (No. VSL-2026-0417, November 2, 2026).** Coverage appears to meet SLA §13.1. The CGL is $2M per occurrence and $4M aggregate; the umbrella is $5M; Tech E&O and cyber are $5M each. Rekaind and its Affiliates are named as additional insureds on the CGL and umbrella, as §13.2 requires. Two points are relevant to other issues:
  - The certificate is "information only." It is partial practical mitigation for Issue 2 but no substitute for an uncapped indemnity.
  - It was issued after the Notice and references the SLA as a live contract. This is consistent with Velert not having accepted the termination (Issue 1).

---

## V. Recommended Immediate Steps

1. **Confirm the facts on the ground.** Determine what Rekaind has done since November 20 regarding payment, invoices, cutover and devices, and whether Velert has responded to the Notice.
2. **Stop any announced non-payment.** Handle disputes under SLA §7.3 or pay under reservation of rights.
3. **Obtain the September and October 2026 Service Reports.** If they qualify, serve a fresh SLS §4.2 notice and a §12.4 breach notice without delay, with a reservation of rights on the October 21 Notice.
4. **Pause or document the migration to replacement systems** until termination is secure, given the §3.4 exclusivity exposure.
5. **Plan for an Ohio forum.** Assume Ohio law and Franklin County venue in assessing litigation risk.
6. **Open renegotiation.** Raise §11.4 and §11.5, Order Form §7 and §15.4, §3.4 and §1.6, §14.2, and §12.2, §1.14 and §12.3. The dispute may give Rekaind leverage for a negotiated exit or a restated agreement.
7. **Docket the non-renewal window.** Calendar December 18, 2027 to January 2, 2028, subject to confirmation.

# MEMORANDUM

**TO:** Supervising Partner
**FROM:** Associate
**DATE:** November 27, 2026
**RE:** Rekaind Vertical Services, Inc.: review of the LiftSense license documents with Velert Systems, LLC (Licensor Ref. VS-REK-2025-001)

---

## I. Scope and Summary

I reviewed all seven documents in the folder:

1. **Software License Agreement** effective March 3, 2025 (the "**SLA**").
2. **Service Level Schedule** (Exhibit A) (the "**SLS**").
3. **Order Form No. 001**, Order Effective Date March 3, 2025 (the "**Order Form**").
4. **Rekaind's letter to Velert** dated October 21, 2026.
5. **Side Letter** dated May 12, 2025.
6. **Rekaind's dispatch-center office lease** at 1700 Spring Garden Street.
7. **Velert's Certificate of Liability Insurance** No. VSL-2026-0417.

The lease and the insurance certificate do not bear on the Velert relationship in any way that raises an issue. They are covered briefly in Part III.

**Key commercial terms:**
- **Licensed Units.** 1,140 elevator and escalator units in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware (Order Form §1.1).
- **Annual Subscription Fee.** $410,400, which is $360 per Licensed Unit per year (Order Form §3.1).
- **Initial Order Term.** 36 months from March 3, 2025, ending March 2, 2028 (Order Form §2.1).

**Order of precedence.** SLA §15.4 ranks the documents as follows: Side Letter, then Order Form, then the SLA, then the SLS. It states expressly that "where any provision of an Order Form conflicts with any provision of the body of this Agreement, the Order Form shall control." The Order Form therefore prevails over the SLA in any conflict, and the Side Letter prevails over both. This ranking drives two of the issues below.

**Issues identified:**

| # | Issue | Location |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Overbroad exclusivity: worldwide, all affiliates, bars in-house development | SLA §3.4; SLA §1.6 |
| 2 | Velert may assign freely, including to a competitor; Rekaind needs consent | SLA §14.2 (cf. §14.1) |
| 3 | Bodily-injury and property-damage indemnity has fallen under the liability cap | Side Letter §2; SLA §11.4 |
| 4 | Ohio law and Franklin County venue override the negotiated Delaware terms | Order Form §7; SLA §15.4 |
| 5 | Automatic 36-month renewals with a 15-day opt-out window and fee escalator | SLA §§12.2, 12.3, 1.14; Order Form §2 |

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Overbroad Exclusivity Covenant

**Location:** SLA §3.4 (Exclusivity), read with SLA §1.6 (definition of "Covered Equipment"). See also SLA §2.5 and Order Form §1.4.

**What the documents say.**
- **SLA §3.4.** For the Term and while any Order Form is in effect, Licensee "shall not license, use, or develop," and shall cause its Affiliates not to license, use or develop, "any remote-monitoring, condition-monitoring, dispatch or work-order software other than the Platform for any Covered Equipment." Rekaind also may not procure monitoring hardware for Covered Equipment that transmits to any other platform.
- **SLA §1.6 and the repeated sentence in §3.4.** Covered Equipment means "any equipment serviced by Licensee or any of its Affiliates anywhere in the world." That covers elevators, escalators, moving walks, dumbwaiters, wheelchair and platform lifts, and their components.
- **The license itself is narrower.** Under SLA §3.1 it is non-exclusive and limited to the Licensed Units, which the Order Form fixes at 1,140 units in PA, NJ and DE. Units outside those three states may be added only by a separate Order Form or a signed amendment (Order Form §1.4).
- **Nothing narrows the definition.** Neither the Order Form nor the Side Letter changes the definition of Covered Equipment.

**Why it matters for Rekaind.**
- **Scope mismatch.** The restriction is far broader than the license. Rekaind pays for 1,140 Mid-Atlantic units but is barred from using any competing monitoring, dispatch or work-order tool on every unit it or any affiliate services, anywhere in the world. That includes units outside the portfolio and units in other states where Rekaind may win new contracts.
- **Customer and OEM mandates.** Building owners and OEMs often require their own remote-monitoring systems as a condition of a contract. Rekaind could not accept those contracts without breaching §3.4. In practice it would have to buy additional LiftSense Order Forms to service new business.
- **No in-house development.** The word "develop" bars Rekaind from building its own dispatch or work-order software. This reaches core business systems that are not monitoring at all.
- **Affiliates and future transactions.** Rekaind must "cause" its Affiliates to comply. Any acquisition or affiliate restructuring would import the restriction into the acquired business.
- **Transition risk.** The covenant runs while any Order Form "remains in effect." Running a replacement system in parallel, or migrating region by region before LiftSense ends, risks a technical breach of §3.4. Rekaind's October 21, 2026 letter (§8.2) contemplates exactly that kind of phased regional cutover to "replacement arrangements."
- **Leverage.** Because the covenant is drafted as exclusivity, a breach would give Velert a material-breach argument under SLA §12.4 and leverage in any dispute.

**Recommended fix.**
- **Narrow the scope.** Amend §3.4 and §1.6 so exclusivity, if it is kept at all, applies only to the Licensed Units under an executed Order Form, and only for that Order Form's Subscription Term.
- **Remove the overreach.** Delete "or develop," the Affiliate covenant, and the "anywhere in the world" language.
- **Add express carve-outs** for:
  - systems mandated by a building owner, customer or OEM;
  - units outside the Order Form territory;
  - Rekaind's internal ERP, CRM and dispatch systems; and
  - parallel running and migration during any notice, wind-down or transition period, including under SLA §12.8.
- **Fallback position.** Convert §3.4 into a "most-favored" or right-of-first-offer commitment for new units within PA, NJ and DE.

---

### Issue 2: One-Sided Assignment Right in Velert's Favor

**Location:** SLA §14.2 (Assignment by Licensor), contrasted with SLA §14.1 (Assignment by Licensee).

**What the documents say.**
- **Rekaind needs consent.** Under SLA §14.1, Rekaind may not assign without Velert's prior written consent, although that consent may not be unreasonably withheld.
- **Velert does not.** Under SLA §14.2, Velert "may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, together with any or all Order Forms, without Licensee's consent." It may assign to any Affiliate, or to any successor to the relevant business or assets "by merger, consolidation, change of control, sale of assets, sale of equity or otherwise."
- **Notice comes after the fact.** Velert need only notify Rekaind within 30 days *after* the assignment takes effect.
- **No exit right.** Rekaind has no right to object and no right to terminate.

**Why it matters for Rekaind.**
- **Competitor risk.** Rekaind is an independent maintenance contractor that competes with the elevator OEMs for maintenance contracts. Remote-monitoring platforms are natural acquisition targets for OEMs. If an OEM acquired Velert, or bought the LiftSense business, that competitor would hold Rekaind's Customer Data and control a platform Rekaind is contractually bound to use (see Issue 1). That data includes customer lists, site and building information, maintenance histories, callback records, technician records and Equipment Data for every Licensed Unit.
- **Existing protections are thin.** The confidentiality and Aggregated Data protections in SLA §§8.4 and 9 bind the assignee as a successor. They would not prevent a competitor from controlling the product roadmap, pricing at renewal (§12.3), service quality or support priorities.
- **Combined effect.** This issue compounds the exclusivity and auto-renewal problems. Rekaind could be locked into a competitor-owned platform with no clean exit.

**Recommended fix.**
- **Mutual standard.** Make §14.2 mutual with §14.1, so that Velert's assignment also requires consent not to be unreasonably withheld. At minimum, require consent for any assignment or change of control involving an elevator or escalator manufacturer or maintenance provider, or any of their affiliates (a "**Competitor**").
- **Exit right.** Add a right for Rekaind to terminate any Order Form without penalty, with a pro-rata refund of prepaid Fees and full §12.8 transition assistance. That right should be exercisable within a defined period (say 120 days) after notice of an assignment to, or change of control in favor of, a Competitor.
- **Advance notice.** Require at least 60 days' notice *before* any assignment or change of control, not 30 days after.
- **Data firewall.** Add covenants that Customer Data and Aggregated Data may not be accessed or used by any Competitor's service business, with audit rights.
- **Lift exclusivity.** Release the exclusivity in §3.4 automatically on any assignment to a Competitor.

### Issue 3: The Side Letter Has Brought Velert's Bodily-Injury Indemnity Under the Cap

**Location:** Side Letter §2 (Restructuring of Licensor Indemnification), read with SLA §11.3 (Limitation of Liability) and SLA §11.4(a) (Exceptions).

**What the documents say.**
- **Original SLA §10.1.** Velert indemnified Rekaind against third-party claims for (a) IP infringement and (b) "bodily injury, death or damage to tangible property caused by any defect, error or failure of the Platform or any Connected Device." Item (b) expressly included failures to deliver entrapment, passenger-alarm or safety-fault alerts.
- **The cap.** SLA §11.3 caps each party's liability at "the Fees paid or payable in the 12 months preceding the claim." Under the Order Form that is roughly $410,400, plus any device and other fees in the period.
- **The carve-out.** SLA §11.4(a) excludes from the cap "Licensor's indemnification obligations under Section 10.1." As originally drafted, that carve-out covered both the IP indemnity and the bodily-injury and property indemnity.
- **The Side Letter restructuring.**
  - Side Letter §2.1 deletes §10.1 and replaces it with a new §10.1, which is a broadened IP indemnity covering more jurisdictions, open-source claims, Platform outputs and Aggregated Data.
  - Side Letter §2.3 adds a **new Section 10.2** for "bodily injury, death or damage to tangible property." The new provision also adds failures of the secondary alert-routing path.
  - Side Letter §2.4 renumbers the remaining provisions, and Annex 1 confirms that old §10.1(b) is now §10.2.
  - The conforming changes in Side Letter §2.5 are confined to Section 10. **Section 11.4 is not amended.**
- **Precedence.** The Side Letter sits at the top of the §15.4 ranking, and Side Letter §9.1 provides that references to "this Agreement" now mean the Agreement as modified.

**Why it matters for Rekaind.**
- **The carve-out now reaches only the IP indemnity.** SLA §11.4(a) still carves out only "indemnification obligations under Section 10.1," and new §10.1 is purely the IP indemnity. Velert's bodily-injury, death and property-damage indemnity in new §10.2 therefore now falls **within** the 12-month-fees cap of about $410,400.
- **The exposure is the most serious in the relationship.** It covers passenger injury or death from a failed entrapment alert, a delayed out-of-service notification or a Connected Device defect. These are the claims most likely to produce seven- or eight-figure verdicts.
- **The cap is aggregate.** A single serious incident could exhaust it.
- **Sequence of claims.** Rekaind, as the maintenance contractor, will typically be the first defendant in a passenger-injury suit. It would then be left to fund most of the defense and settlement itself.
- **How it happened.** The restructuring looks neutral, and the IP changes are favorable. But its practical effect is to remove the most valuable protection in the indemnity package. Under Side Letter §1.4, the change applies to Third-Party Claims first asserted on or after May 12, 2025. That includes any claim arising from the June to August 2026 alert-delivery incidents described in Rekaind's October 21, 2026 letter.
- **Insurance does not solve the contract problem.** Velert's certificate shows $2M/$4M CGL and $5M umbrella coverage, with Rekaind and its Affiliates as additional insureds for "your product" and completed operations (Certificate §§6, 8, 13). That additional-insured coverage is a useful separate route to recovery. However, SLA §13.4 says insurance does not limit liability, and coverage is subject to policy terms and exhaustion. It is not a substitute for an uncapped contractual indemnity.

**Recommended fix.**
- **Amend §11.4(a).** It should read: "Licensor's indemnification obligations under Sections 10.1 and 10.2 (as those Sections are numbered following the Side Letter dated May 12, 2025)."
- **Make the amendment retroactive.** It should apply from the Side Letter Effective Date, so that no claim falls into the gap.
- **Fix §11.5 as well.** Section 11.5 cross-refers to §11.4(a), so confirm that consequential damages are also not excluded for §10.2 claims.
- **Check every cross-reference.** Review all cross-references to Section 10 in the SLA, including §§5.4, 12.9 and 15.12, against the renumbering.
- **Negotiating position.** Velert's stated intent was a neutral restructuring, so we should present this as a drafting correction. Velert may nonetheless resist. If it insists on a cap, it should be a separate, high super-cap for §10.2 claims that is at least equal to the insurance limits, about $7M, and not the 12-month-fees figure.
- **Preserve the record.** Ask the client to locate the May 2025 negotiation correspondence. It may support a mutual-mistake or reformation argument if Velert refuses to amend.

### Issue 4: Order Form Choice of Ohio Law and Forum Overrides the Delaware Terms

**Location:** Order Form §7.1 (Governing Law) and §7.2 (Venue), read with SLA §15.4 (Order of Precedence). These conflict with SLA §15.1 (Governing Law) and §15.2 (Forum).

**What the documents say.**
- **The SLA's choice.** SLA §15.1 chooses Delaware law. SLA §15.2 gives exclusive jurisdiction to the state or federal courts in Wilmington, Delaware.
- **The Order Form's choice.** Order Form §7.1 states that "this Order Form **and the Agreement**" are governed by "the laws of the State of Ohio." Order Form §7.2 submits both parties to the exclusive jurisdiction and venue of "the state and federal courts located in Franklin County, Ohio" for any proceeding relating to the Order Form *or the Agreement*. Franklin County is Velert's home county (Columbus).
- **Precedence.** Under SLA §15.4, "where any provision of an Order Form conflicts with any provision of the body of this Agreement, the Order Form shall control."

**Why it matters for Rekaind.**
- **The Delaware terms are displaced.** Read together, the two provisions mean the Ohio choice controls. The Delaware governing law and neutral forum that Rekaind appears to have negotiated are effectively replaced, and the Ohio clause reaches the entire SLA, not just the Order Form.
- **Practical cost.** Any dispute with Velert would be litigated in Velert's home court, under Velert's home-state law. That includes disputes over service levels, refunds, Service Credits, indemnity or the cap issue above. Rekaind would bear travel and local-counsel cost and lose home-forum advantage. Because the jury-trial waiver in §15.3 is untouched, the case would also be tried to an Ohio bench.
- **Uncertainty.** Velert may argue the Order Form controls. Rekaind may argue the clauses can be harmonized, or that the Order Form clause was boilerplate. That ambiguity is itself a litigation cost and could produce a threshold forum fight before the merits are reached.
- **Analysis must change.** The analysis of several provisions changes under Ohio law, including the limitation of liability, indemnity construction and the enforceability of the exclusivity covenant. Our advice should be checked under Ohio law, not only Delaware.
- **Future Order Forms.** Every future Order Form on Velert's paper could carry the same clause.

**Recommended fix.**
- **Delete Order Form §7** by written amendment under SLA §15.9.
- **Carve out key terms from §15.4.** Amend §15.4 so that governing law, forum, limitation of liability, indemnity and assignment in the SLA body prevail over any Order Form unless the Order Form expressly identifies the SLA section it overrides and states the intent to override it.
- **Fallback.** If Velert will not accept Delaware, propose a neutral forum, or Pennsylvania as Rekaind's home jurisdiction where the Licensed Units are concentrated. Consider whether arbitration with a neutral seat would suit the client.
- **Until amended.** In the meantime, assume Ohio law and a Franklin County forum when assessing any dispute with Velert.

### Issue 5: Automatic 36-Month Renewal with a 15-Day Opt-Out Window

**Location:** SLA §12.2 (Renewal of Order Forms), read with SLA §1.14 (Non-Renewal Window), SLA §12.3 (Renewal Pricing), and Order Form §§2.1 and 2.2.

**What the documents say.**
- **Automatic renewal.** Under SLA §12.2, each Order Form "automatically renews for a successive term of the same length," a "Renewal Term equal in length to the Initial Order Term," and renews again at the end of each Renewal Term.
- **The renewal term is 36 months.** The Initial Order Term under the Order Form is 36 months (§2.1), so each Renewal Term is also 36 months. Order Form §2.2 incorporates §12.2.
- **A 15-day opt-out window.** Non-renewal notice is effective only during the Non-Renewal Window. That window is defined in SLA §1.14 and repeated in §12.2 as "not more than seventy-five (75) days and not less than sixty (60) days" before expiry. Rekaind therefore has a 15-day window to opt out.
- **Fee escalator.** Under SLA §12.3, Velert may raise per-unit fees by up to 7% for each Renewal Term on 90 days' notice.

**Why it matters for Rekaind.**
- **Applied to the current Order Form.** The Initial Order Term ends March 2, 2028. Non-renewal notice must be delivered between about **December 18, 2027 and January 2, 2028**, a window that falls over the year-end holidays.
- **Missing the window is costly.** Notice given early (before December 18, 2027) or late (after January 2, 2028) is ineffective. Rekaind would be committed through March 2, 2031 at up to $439,128 a year, which is $410,400 plus 7%. Repeated cycles compound.
- **Minimum unit floor.** The 1,000-unit minimum commitment (Order Form §1.5) continues through any renewal. This limits Rekaind's ability to shrink the portfolio.
- **Lock-in compounds.** Combined with the exclusivity covenant (Issue 1) and Velert's free assignment right (Issue 2), a missed window could lock Rekaind into three more years on a platform owned by a competitor.
- **No easy exit.** There is no termination for convenience in the SLA.

**Recommended fix.**
- **Shorter renewals.** Amend §12.2 so that renewals run for 12 months.
- **A real notice period.** Replace the §1.14 window with a simple outside deadline: notice "at any time up to 60 days before expiration." Alternatively, allow Rekaind to terminate for convenience during any Renewal Term on 90 days' notice.
- **Reminder obligation.** Require Velert to send written renewal notice, with pricing, 120 to 150 days before expiry. Renewal should be conditional on that notice being given.
- **Tighter pricing.** Cap renewal increases at the lower of 3% and CPI, and require the §12.3 price notice to be delivered before the Non-Renewal Window opens.
- **Immediate step.** Docket the December 18, 2027 to January 2, 2028 window now, and build similar windows for any future Order Form into the client's contract calendar.
